entries.title: Democrats Snagged Control Over Trump’s Judicial Picks
entries.summary: The incoming Senate majority can wield the confirmation process to shape the last stage of the president’s judicial legacy.
entries.content:
Tuesday's blue wave gives Democrats an unexpected foothold to leave a mark on the nation's judicial system — including the Supreme Court.

After two years of Republicans approving President Donald Trump's judicial picks, the Democrats in January will seize control of the confirmation process for the last two years of his presidency.

Republicans could try to ram through as many of the 21 pending conservative appointees while they still can for district and appeals courts, which have lifetime appointments and increasingly determine the fate of many presidential policies.

One of the judges confirmed in Trump's lame-duck period in 2020, for example, was U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, who would ultimately dismiss the Mar-a-Lago-based criminal case against him.

Democrats this year have criticized Trump's judicial nominees, in part because many have declined to say Trump lost the 2020 presidential election.

Once the new session starts, Democrats could reject Trump nominees they find too extreme, negotiate for more moderate nominees or let vacancies stack up for a potential Democratic president in 2028, experts say.

Trump is “going to have to play ball with the Democratic senators," said Russell Wheeler, who tracks judicial nominations at the progressive Brookings Institution. "I don't think they're in a position to be too accommodating to Trump. A few may squeak through, but not many.”

Jeremy Fogel, a former federal judge who is a member of the nonpartisan Keep Our Republic’s Article III Coalition focused on judicial independence, recalled his own Senate confirmation in 1998 with President Bill Clinton and a Republican Senate.

“We've been here before,” he said. “It's not like there’s a total embargo of nominations. People who get confirmed are not as offensive to the other side. The only people who were getting through were those with bipartisan credentials. What you tend to get is more moderate people with a broad consensus that this person would be a good Article III judge. That's my hopeful view of this.”

At the same time, the election outcome also led to speculation that the conservative Supreme Court justices Clarence Thomas or Samuel Alito could quickly resign so Trump and Republicans can confirm a successor with a similar ideology before the end of the year.

But court watchers downplayed the possibility Wednesday. Thomas is close to becoming the longest-serving justice in history. And Alito said to CBS News recently that at age 76 he had “thought about” retiring but told The Wall Street Journal he decided to stay “here for another term.”

"No justice is going to announce in the next few days that he will be stepping down at the end of the Court’s term. Justices don’t make snap decisions about retiring," Edward Whelan, a lawyer at the conservative Ethics and Public Policy Center, said in a Substack post.

Another reason: Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown fills the empty Ohio Senate seat next month, and at least five Republicans senators — including three Trump essentially pushed out — “aren’t going to be eager to do Trump any favors.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis was one Republican who pointed out that the next few weeks could be the last window for years when it comes to the Supreme Court, and that Democrats might be in control of the Senate for some time. He put the chance at "zero" that Democrats would confirm a Republican president’s pick for the high court, and "probably zero" through 2033.

The contentious confirmation showdowns over Supreme Court nominations would leave Democrats unlikely to allow Trump to fill an unplanned vacancy, such as illness or death of a conservative justices.

That could leave the court, currently with a 6-3 conservative tilt, with eight members and unable to decide cases if evenly split — a possibility Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller referred to in a social media post.

Muller half expects the next two years to look a lot like President Barack Obama’s final chapter, in which then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell blocked his court picks in an attempt to hold out on the possibility of a Republican presidential successor.

That winning bet paid off when Trump inherited an outsized backlog of nominations during his first administration, including a Supreme Court vacancy left by the death of Justice Antonin Scalia.

“I’d look at that precedent and wonder if that's what [Democratic senators] Sheldon Whitehouse and Chuck Schumer want to do,” Muller said.

Muller noted that as of late “we expect our judges to do a lot of work, especially on executive orders and hot-button, short-fuse litigation.” A flood of court battles on constitutional issues has vastly raised the stakes and put Trump’s own legacy in jeopardy, potentially incentivizing either side to hold their ground in the two years that remain in the presidential administration.

“We've put a lot of strain on the courts, and understandably there's a reason why senators and the president are very picky about who gets to those positions. It will certainly create additional strain on the judiciary,” Muller said.

entries.title: Leon Black Sues Rep. Robert Garcia Over Epstein Comments
entries.summary: The court filing comes less than two months after the House approved a resolution holding Black in contempt of Congress for defying the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas in its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein.
entries.content:
NEW YORK (AP) — Billionaire Leon Black on Wednesday filed a federal defamation lawsuit against California Rep. Robert Garcia for public comments the Democratic congressman made tying him to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

The court filing comes less than two months after the House approved a resolution holding Black in contempt of Congress for defying the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas in its investigation into Epstein.

In June, Black appeared for a voluntary interview at the committee during which he denied any knowledge of Epstein's sex trafficking network.

Weeks later, Garcia said during a TV interview that “Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes” and that Black “was one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before he committed suicide in prison.

In addition, Garcia said that he had “talked to survivors that have credibly named Leon Black as someone that was involved in direct abuse of women and was directly involved" with Epstein.

Those statements were false and were made maliciously, Black asserts through his lawyers. The defamation lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York seeks a jury trial and $7.25 million in compensatory and punitive damages.

“Congressman Garcia’s knowing lies have caused real and significant ongoing harm to Mr. Black. His physical safety has been threatened, he has received a barrage of hateful calls, emails, and social media posts, and his business and philanthropic endeavors have suffered,” the filing states.

Garcia’s office didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.

In September, Garcia called the contempt resolution against Black “an important step toward justice and accountability.”

Black had refused to respond to subpoenas asking him to appear and to turn over any potential nondisclosure agreements involving the investigation into Epstein.

Black's lawyers have repeatedly denounced the Oversight Committee's pursuit of the former head of a private equity firm as an abuse of congressional power. They have maintained he had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s criminal conduct.

Black was among several prominent figures, including Bill Clinton and Bill Gates, who had been asked to appear as part of the Oversight Committee's long-running probe of Epstein. Survivors of Epstein’s alleged sexual abuse have told personal stories of being young women in a trafficking enterprise organized by Epstein and his colleague Ghislaine Maxwell.

Black co-founded the private equity firm Apollo Global Management and stepped down in 2021 during the fallout over his ties to Epstein.

Lawmakers have alleged that Black paid Epstein $180 million during their yearslong relationship.

A 2021 review commissioned by Apollo found that Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to soliciting prostitution from a minor. The review said the payments were for “bona fide tax, estate planning and other related services.”

entries.title: Hawks Down Wizards, 120-105
entries.summary: Nickeil Alexander-Walker scored 26 points to lead the Hawks to a victory over the Wizards.
entries.content:
By Ian Nicholas Quillen

Nickeil Alexander-Walker scored 26 points to lead the Atlanta Hawks to a 120-105 victory over the Washington Wizards and former Hawks star guard Trae Young on Wednesday night.

Alexander-Walker hit six 3-pointers after sinking a career-high-tying nine in a 104-102 win at Indiana on Monday.

Onyeka Okongwu added 14 points and 16 rebounds for the Hawks in their first time playing against Young, who finished with 18 points, since trading the four-time All-Star to the Wizards in January.

CJ McCollum and Aaron Wiggins scored 15 points each to help Atlanta make up for All-Star forward Jalen Johnson missing his second straight game with a sprained left ankle.

Anthony Davis had 26 points and 10 rebounds for Washington.

Kyshawn George added 25 points for the Wizards, who trailed throughout the final three quarters.

Atlanta built its game-high lead of 16 in the second with a 13-0 run.

Asa Newell hit a tip-in at the first-quarter buzzer, and Zuby Ejiofor hit two transition baskets, prompting a quick timeout from Wizards coach Brian Keefe. But the surge continued, with Kingston Flemings hitting a runner and Wiggins sinking a 3-pointer before Dyson Daniels' driving layup made it 48-32 with 9:06 left in the half.

Washington closed within seven by halftime and cut it to four twice in the third, the latter time on Young's step-back 3 to make it 83-79.

But Corey Kispert — a player Atlanta received when dealing Young — converted a four-point play on the following possession, and the game never got closer than six afterward.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: When the Party’s Over
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 3, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: What’s next for JLG, the council’s at-large vacancy and Tom Sietsema’s favorite fast food.

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 7/10. A few showers, but we could probably use some rain. Still plenty warm for November. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

The celebrations have ended and now the real work begins.

That’s both the message and a reality for D.C. mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George, who’s coming off of Tuesday’s resounding victory with a sobering task ahead of her: running a city facing significant challenges.

Lewis George’s ambitious platform — which includes cheaper child care, more housing and much more — is running headfirst into an expected budget deficit for the next fiscal year that could exceed $800 million. She’ll be tasked with finding money for social programs she has long championed, while at the same time typing to advance her own initiatives.

That harsh fiscal reality may push Lewis George to focus on smaller goals, like improving city services, The Washington Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports. “We will pick up the trash, plow the snow, eliminate the rats and make it easier to open a small business and easier to keep it open,” she told supporters on Tuesday night. (Never underestimate the impact of taking on rats.)

At least she’ll have a friendly Congress to work with, avoiding the aggressive Republican interference into D.C.’s local affairs that the city has experienced over the last two years. And that Democratic control could bring quick dividends for D.C. by way of lifting certain prohibitions on how the city can spend its own money, including on legalizing recreational marijuana and subsidizing abortions for low-income women.

The unpredictable factor will be President Donald Trump. There’s already been friction between the two, and Lewis George’s brand was partly built on standing up to him more than she said Mayor Muriel Bowser did. If Trump feels like he’s lost control elsewhere, he may exercise it where we’ve already seen it most: in renovating D.C. Still, Lewis George says she’s open to working with him where there’s a shared benefit for the city; her team says they’ve already reached out to set up a meeting.

The JLG machinery has kicked into high gear already. As The Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports, on Wednesday she announced the transition team that will lead her through the two-month sprint before her inauguration in January.

Voss-JLGwatchparty_42.jpg (8640x5760, AR: 1.50)



FROM THE DISTRICT

“There ain’t no certainty here,” a folksy D.C. Council Chair Phil Mendelson told The Sun when asked what’s come of the political drama involving the vacant at-large council seat once occupied by Robert White. As The Sun’s Metro team reported Tuesday, At-Large council member Christina Henderson has made a play for the seat, but the D.C. Democratic Party counters that only it has the legal right to appoint an interim replacement.

Sleep through Tuesday’s results? If you’re feeling out of the loop, or just want a round-up of the DMV’s pivotal races, The Sun’s Kendall Staton has you covered.

Speaking of electoral representation… D.C. youths want some. Young members of a local nonprofit are hoping to create a new youth governing council in the District that could weigh in on legislation brought before the D.C. Council, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports.

Clearing the rough: Trump administration officials are expected to file a brief by 5 p.m. today explaining why they can’t disclose when tree removals or a links-style golf design were first added to the proposal for the redevelopment of East Potomac, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes ordered the Justice Department to explain itself in an Oct. 30 hearing after Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told Reyes an Interior Department official had “put pen to paper” for the proposal weeks before it was sent to the National Capital Planning Commission — a marked change from what he had told the court on Oct. 19 about the timing of the project.

A D.C. man was arrested for pretending to shoot at National Guard troops with a “finger gun” this week, The Washington Post reports. He was charged with “threats in a menacing manner” and assaulting a police officer. It’s been a tense year between D.C. residents and Guard members, whose presence here is normalized for some but still frequent cause for protest and ongoing litigation.





FROM MARYLAND

The public outcry over data center development in Calvert County this past year is a

microcosm of a larger movement found in communities across the country. Those debates might just be a catalyst for rejuvenating local civic life, Anusha Mathur writes for Washington Sun Perspectives.

Running it back: Rep. Jamie Raskin is poised to become the first Marylander to chair the U.S. House Judiciary Committee in nearly 200 years, and he’s not afraid to pursue another impeachment of Trump, The Baltimore Banner reports.





TALK TO TOM


Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here. 

Do you have a favorite fast-food meal?

Regular readers know the crisp-golden answer to this one: I have a soft spot for Popeyes (spicy) fried chicken, which I gravitate to on holidays, specifically New Year’s Eve, and whenever I’m celebrating something. Indeed, my colleagues trotted out Popeyes at my farewell party at The Washington Post last year (with champagne instead of my usual Coke to wash back the pleasure).

Much of the appeal of fast food is consistency. Popeyes chicken, which originated in Louisiana in 1972, is reliably crunchy, juicy and peppery (in the case of the spicy version). The fresh-tasting coleslaw and soothing red beans and rice are my picks among the sides, along with the obligatory flaky biscuits — albeit only when they’re warm.

The only other fast food that comes close to that affection is the Filet-O-Fish from McDonald’s, something I indulge in once a year or so.

In the full Q&A: protocol for talking on the phone in a restaurant, the Phoenix food scene and holiday restaurant picks





SPORTS

Trinity Rodman AP - 26197361108152 (5000x3374, AR: 1.48)One major reason why the Spirit have a playoff game this weekend? Trinity Rodman has turned in the best and healthiest season of her career, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports. The 24-year-old forward has started every match, producing 12 goals and eight assists. Steady and seasoned, she’s also taken on a bigger leadership role.

“I’m very happy and very proud, to be honest,” coach Adrián González said recently. “She’s been working very, very hard behind the scenes … being more resilient, and also, I think, being more mature.”

The Commanders’ injury woes continue. Coach Dan Quinn said on Wednesday that defensive tackles Daron Payne (foot) and Javon Kinlaw (knee) and running back Jeremy McNichols (foot) are all likely out for the season. In corresponding moves, the team elevated defensive tackle Ricky Barber from the practice squad and claimed former back Robert Henry Jr. off waivers.





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Gaby Morera Di Núbila.
